n: In this lecture we consider hypoxia and its types. At rest the body needs 6-8 L of air per minute; with physical exertion the requirement rises 10-20 times. In the central nervous system, cessation of tissue respiration for 5-10 minutes leads to irreversible changes, whereas in muscle and connective tissue this period is considerably longer. Hypoxia may be exogenous or endogenous. The exogenous types are hypoxic, hyperoxic and hypercapnic; the endogenous types are respiratory, haemic, circulatory, cytotoxic and physiological.

t: Types of hypoxia and speed of development
n: Types of hypoxia and speed of development. In the hypoxic form the oxygen in the air is below 20.93%: in the mountains, that is, hypobaric; in a mixture low in oxygen, that is, normobaric; at depth under water, that is, in hyperbaric conditions. Hypercapnic hypoxia is observed in a confined space: oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises. By speed of development, hypoxia is fulminant, acute, subacute or chronic. The fulminant form develops in seconds, the acute in minutes, and the subacute in hours. For forensic medicine the fulminant and acute forms are important.

Endogenous hypoxia is divided into five types. In the respiratory type the cause is compression of the neck organs, closure of the airways and orifices, compression of the chest and abdomen, or damage to the lungs or respiratory centre. Circulatory hypoxia develops in disturbance of the circulation. Haemic hypoxia occurs when haemoglobin is reduced or oxygen binding is impaired, that is, in poisonings. Cytotoxic, that is, tissue, hypoxia arises mainly in poisonings from impairment of tissue respiration. Physiological hypoxia is temporary and is associated with physical exertion or a heavy meal.

Asphyxia and mechanical asphyxia. The word asphyxia is Greek and means “absence of pulse”: a is negation, sphygmos is pulse. Asphyxia is an acute disturbance of the activity of vital systems due to lack of oxygen and accumulation of carbon dioxide as a result of impaired external respiration. A state arising from impaired external respiration under the action of a mechanical factor is called mechanical asphyxia. In it hypoxia develops together with hypercapnia.

Classification of mechanical asphyxia. According to the forensic medical classification, mechanical asphyxia is divided into three types: asphyxia from compression, from closure, and asphyxia in a confined space. In asphyxia from compression, if the neck organs are compressed it is called strangulation asphyxia, and if the chest and abdominal organs are compressed, compression asphyxia. Asphyxia from closure includes closure of the respiratory orifices, closure of the airways and drowning.

Autoerotic asphyxia, that is, sexual asphyxia. It occurs in persons inclined to sexual deviations, mainly lone middle-aged men; the arousal takes place under conditions of hypoxia and hypercapnia. The process is controlled with the hands, feet and devices; often the neck is compressed by a ligature or a polythene bag is put over the head. Sometimes the state ends in death and is assessed as an accident. At the scene, objects confirming the sexual deviation are found.

The course of asphyxia. The preasphyxial period lasts on average 20-30 seconds: breathing stops briefly, then slows, and the organism mobilises its compensatory capacities. In compensation the amount of circulating blood increases, the blood becomes thinner and is redistributed in favour of vital organs. The asphyxial period consists of five stages. Its course depends on the type and intensity of the asphyxial factor, and also on the health of the organism. Loss of consciousness occurs in 40-60 seconds.

Stages of the asphyxial period. The first stage is inspiratory dyspnoea, about 1 minute: breathing quickens, blood pressure falls, venous pressure rises, and consciousness is lost in 40-60 seconds. The second stage is expiratory dyspnoea, about 1 minute: expiration strengthens, clonic convulsions occur, and passing of urine, semen and faeces is possible. The third stage is a brief pause, 30-40 seconds. The fourth is terminal breathing, up to 5 minutes. In the fifth stage breathing stops completely, while the heart may beat for another 3-10 minutes.

t: Mechanism of death and reflex cardiac arrest
n: The mechanism of death and reflex cardiac arrest. In death from mechanical asphyxia, along with hypoxia of the brain, cardiac arrest is also important. Reflex arrest occurs from irritation of the receptors of the carotid sinuses, larynx, trachea and bronchi, or from injury to the vagus and superior laryngeal nerves. Remember: in reflex arrest within 30 seconds the general asphyxial signs do not have time to develop and may not be detected in the corpse.

The postasphyxial state. If asphyxia does not end in death, for example when a drowning person is rescued or a hanged person is taken down from the ligature, a complex of changes called the postasphyxial state remains in the body. It consists of four periods: asphyxial coma, stupor, disorientation and memory impairment, and residual effects. In the period of coma, atony of the muscles, dilatation of the pupils and absence of reflexes are observed. Then decerebrate rigidity and tonic and tonic-clonic convulsions appear. Residual effects include paresis, paralysis and headache.

Consequences of the postasphyxial state. In mild cases the changes disappear without residue in 1-2 weeks with medical care. In other cases impairment of memory and attention, headache, paresis and paralysis may remain. With asphyxia of 3 minutes or more, persistent hypotension, ischaemia of the internal organs and sometimes myocardial infarction are observed. Pulmonary oedema in the first hours is regarded as an unfavourable prognostic sign. In the first minutes and hours death results from asphyxial coma, in the first day from oedema of the lungs and brain, and later from hypostatic pneumonia.

t: General external signs of mechanical asphyxia
n: General external signs of mechanical asphyxia. Cyanosis of the face and neck is not constant: it may disappear when the corpse lies on its back, and appear without asphyxia when it lies face down. Extensive bluish-violet cadaveric lividity forms rapidly within an hour after death, because the blood is fluid and saturated with carbon dioxide. In the conjunctiva there are small haemorrhages, that is, subconjunctival ecchymoses. Dilatation of the pupils is relatively inconstant. During convulsions, passing of urine, faeces and semen is possible.

Internal signs of mechanical asphyxia. The heart and large veins contain dark red fluid blood. The right chambers of the heart are more filled with blood than the left, which is called the asphyxial heart; venous congestion is found in the internal organs. Beneath the visceral pleura and epicardium there are small, 2-3 mm, dark red haemorrhages, Tardieu's spots. They are located between the lobes of the lungs, on the diaphragmatic pleura and on the posterior surface of the heart. An anaemic, contracted spleen is called Sabinsky's sign; it arises from the discharge of blood from the depot in the preasphyxial period.

Strangulation asphyxia: hanging. Strangulation asphyxia makes up more than two thirds of deaths from mechanical asphyxia. Hanging is the most frequent type and accounts for 65-70% of deaths from asphyxia. In most cases it is a method of suicide, and as an accident it is a rarity. In typical, that is, complete hanging, the body hangs freely in the ligature. In atypical, that is, incomplete hanging, part of the body has support.

The ligature and its knot. In hanging with support on the knees, the ligature is tightened with a force equal to 20% of body mass. In a lying position, only with a force equal to the mass of the head, that is, 4-5 kg. The ligature may be of soft material, for example a towel, scarf or tie; semi-rigid, for example rope or belt; or rigid, for example wire or chain. The knot has criminalistic significance: when the ligature is removed the knot is not disturbed, and the ligature is cut on the opposite side. The knot may be typical, that is, at the back, or atypical, that is, at the front and side.

There are four factors of death in hanging. The first is narrowing of the airway by compression of the neck: the base of the tongue is displaced towards the pharyngeal wall, and only in some cases is the passage closed completely. The second is compression of the jugular veins: the outflow of blood from the brain is impeded, while the inflow of blood through the vertebral arteries raises intracranial pressure. The third is reflex action: compression of the vagus nerve, the superior laryngeal nerve and the sinocarotid node leads to reflex arrest in heart disease. The fourth is injury to the spinal cord. With an atypical knot, vomiting and aspiration are also possible.

The strangulation furrow. In hanging the main forensic medical sign is the strangulation furrow on the neck; in essence it is an abrasion and depends on the properties of the ligature. In incomplete asphyxia the furrow of a semi-rigid ligature persists for 10-15 days. The position, direction, continuity, width, depth, density and relief of the furrow are studied and compared with the ligature.

t: Features of the furrow in typical hanging
n: Features of the furrow in typical hanging. In typical hanging the furrow is in the upper part of the neck, above the hyoid bone, in an obliquely vertical direction; in atypical hanging it is lower. A rigid ligature leaves a denser and deeper furrow, more evident on the side opposite the knot. The furrow of a semi-rigid ligature is distinct and persists for 10-15 days. With a soft ligature the external furrow may not be visible, but on internal examination a whitish streak is found in the soft tissues, the “copper wire sign”, Casper.

Internal injuries in hanging. Injury of the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage is not characteristic of hanging; it may be seen when the ligature is placed lower. Retropharyngeal haemorrhage is called Brouardel's sign. Signs of stretching: rupture of the intima of the carotid artery, Amussat; haemorrhage in the outer coat, Martin; at the lower end of the muscle, Walcher; into the discs, Simon. Such injuries are observed mainly in obese people in typical hanging with a jerk.

t: Determining the vitality of the furrow
n: Determining the vitality of the furrow. The first step: a flap of skin from the furrow area is cleaned of subcutaneous fat and examined in transmitted light between two glass slides. The second step: congestion and haemorrhages in the area of the ridge indicate vitality, which is Bokarius's test. On microscopy, disturbance of circulation, that is, Neyding's sign, and reactive inflammation, that is, Kasyanov's sign, confirm that the furrow was inflicted during life.

Ligature strangulation. Unlike hanging, here the ligature is tightened not by body weight but by an outside force. In most cases it is homicide, sometimes an accident, for example a scarf caught in machinery, and rarely suicide. The reflexogenic zones are irritated more, so death may result from reflex arrest before the signs of asphyxia have developed fully. The furrow is horizontal, usually at the level of the thyroid cartilage or lower, and often closed. Injury of the hyoid bone is not characteristic, and the signs of Amussat, Walcher and Simon are absent.

Manual strangulation is usually a sign of homicide, in which reflex cardiac arrest is observed more often. On the neck, round or oval bruises remain from the fingers, and arc-shaped abrasions from the nails. In strangulation with both hands from the front, there is one mark on each side on the anterior surface and 2-4 at the back. Internal injuries are more pronounced than external ones: fractures of the horns of the hyoid bone, of the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, and haemorrhages into the soft tissues. In strangulation through a soft object there may be no external marks.

Blunt object and positional asphyxia. In strangulation with blunt objects, for example a stick or the back of a chair, the injuries are in the projection of the area of action. They consist of a bruise, abrasion, haemorrhage, and injury of the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage. Positional asphyxia develops when the head is held flexed for a long time, mainly in persons who are unconscious or unable to perceive; there is no strangulation furrow. Its diagnosis is based on the circumstances of the incident and exclusion of other causes of death.

t: Obturation asphyxia: closure of the respiratory orifices
n: Obturation asphyxia: closure of the respiratory orifices. Obturation asphyxia is divided into closure of the respiratory orifices and closure of the airways. Closing the mouth and nose with a hand or a soft object is used in homicide of young children or weakened adults. Accidental closure occurs mainly in unconscious persons. If there is no resistance, there are no specific signs apart from the general asphyxial signs. With resistance, there are bruises and abrasions around the mouth and nose and haemorrhage in the gum mucosa.

Closure of the airways. The obstructing substances are of three kinds: foreign bodies, for example a fruit stone, button, bone, part of a toy, or dental prosthesis; loose substances, for example sand or flour; and liquids, for example blood or vomit. In most cases it is an accident. The mechanism of death: difficulty in the passage of air, reflex spasm of the vocal cords from irritation of the laryngeal receptors, or reflex cardiac arrest. In alcohol and drug intoxication and in head injury the swallowing and cough reflexes are impaired, and the tendency to aspiration of vomit and blood increases.

Drowning: types and mechanism. Drowning is closure of the airways by liquid. Among deaths from mechanical asphyxia it is in second place after hanging; more than 300 thousand deaths a year are observed worldwide. In most cases it is an accident, in some cases suicide, and rarely homicide. By the degree of water entry, the true, that is, aspiration or “wet”; the asphyxial, that is, spastic or “dry”; and mixed types are distinguished.

Signs of true drowning. Around the mouth and nose there is persistent white fine-bubbled foam, which is Krushevsky's sign; later, because of haemolysis, it takes on a pink tint. The lungs are in a state of hyperhydria, doughy, increased in volume and “marbled”. Beneath the visceral pleura are the Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots, and on the epicardium they are absent. Because of haemodilution and osmotic haemolysis, the cadaveric lividity is pinkish-reddish, and the blood of the left heart is lighter than that of the right, which is Casper's sign.

Additional signs of drowning. About 100 ml of fluid in the abdominal cavity is called Moro's sign, and up to 300 ml of water in the stomach Fegerlund's sign. Sharp movements in an attempt at rescue lead to haemorrhages into the muscles of the neck, chest and back, which is Paltauf's sign. There is a difference between fresh and salt water. In fresh water the blood is diluted and haemolysis occurs. In salt water the osmotic pressure is high: the fluid part of the blood passes into the alveoli, and hypovolaemia and blood thickening develop; Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots are absent.

Asphyxial drowning. Because of laryngospasm, water does not pass into the airways; cyanosis and subconjunctival haemorrhages are marked, while the foam is scanty and unstable. The lungs are sharply emphysematous, that is, in a state of hyperaeration; only Tardieu's spots are present. In the lungs there is no water or foreign matter, and no haemodilution or osmotic haemolysis. Examination for air embolism is Suntsov's test: the left ventricle is punctured. Lymphaemia is found in the thoracic duct, and the stomach may contain up to 1 L of water.

t: Death in water and determining vitality
n: Death in water and determining vitality. Immediately on entering the water, reflex arrest of the heart and breathing is possible; this is “sudden death in water”. In this case pathological changes are found in the internal organs, first of all in the heart. To establish vitality, examination for diatom plankton is carried out: in true drowning the plankton passes into the blood and is found in the parenchymatous organs and bone marrow. The plankton must correspond to that of the water body; a water sample of 1 L is taken. Diatoms in lung tissue have no diagnostic significance.

t: Other laboratory methods and signs of stay in water
n: Other laboratory methods and signs of a stay in water. In the laboratory, pseudoplankton with polarisation microscopy, water bacteria, that is, Pseudomonas putida and fluorescens, as well as cryoscopic, refractometric and electrical conductivity methods are used. Signs of a stay in water: the clothing and body are soiled with silt, cool quickly, and “goose skin” appears. Within a few hours the fingers shrivel, in 2-5 days the palms, in 5-8 days the soles. In 2-3 weeks the skin separates as “gloves of death”, and in 10-15 days the hair is pulled out easily. These changes do not depend on the causes of death.

Compression asphyxia. It develops when the chest and abdomen are compressed by blunt objects. It is often found in natural accidents, for example earthquakes and avalanches, in technogenic incidents, for example building collapse, and also in crowd crushes. Frontal compression of the body is more dangerous than lateral; when the chest and abdomen are compressed together death is faster, and the organism is more resistant to compression of the abdomen alone. Characteristic signs: haemorrhages in the region of the face, neck and upper chest, the “ecchymotic mask”, Olivier-Danger; “carmine swelling” of the lungs, Lacassagne's sign.

t: Asphyxia in a confined closed space
n: Asphyxia in a confined closed space. Here oxygen gradually falls and carbon dioxide rises. At 0.5% in the air breathing quickens, in adults death occurs at 8-10%, and for children even 2.0-2.5% is dangerous. Usually it is an accident: an earthquake, an avalanche, a submarine in distress, a refrigerator chamber, an airtight chest. Putting a plastic bag over the head is regarded as a method of homicide. In partly enclosed places, that is, a deep well, a silo, wine containers, the toxic substances formed in fermentation and putrefaction are also significant.

Introduction to forensic toxicology. The main task of the forensic medical practitioner is to determine the role of a substance, that is, a drug, in the disturbance or death concerned. This is complicated by the fact that physicians, toxicologists and legislators do not sufficiently understand the main questions of forensic science. What is now required is familiarity not with exotic poisons but with the effects of frequently abused substances: stimulants, opiates, cannabinoids and solvents.

Toxic and lethal dose, LD50. The term “toxic” is used in different ways. The lethal dose is expressed in g, µg or mg per kg, but sensitivity differs from person to person. LD50 is the dose at which 50% of those who take it die; it depends on the route of administration, that is, bioavailability: intravenously 100% passes, whereas orally it varies. The results of animal experiments cannot be transferred directly to humans. The courts of many countries do not regard animal studies alone as proof of causation.

Receptors, tolerance and dependence. Drugs act by binding to receptors; oxycodone is much stronger than morphine because it fits the mu receptor better. Tolerance is a rise in dose and weakening of effect on chronic exposure; the effective dose may rise 100-1000-fold, and with cocaine it begins with the first dose. Dependence is the inability to function normally without the substance. In withdrawal, stopping benzodiazepines can lead to uncontrollable convulsions and death.

Materials for examination: general principles. A substance can be detected and quantified in any tissue. The main thing is the interpretation of the result. Detection proves intake, but not toxicity or intent. The site from which a blood sample is taken determines the result: after death, weakly basic substances, for example cocaine, are higher in the left heart than in the right, and higher in the heart than in the leg. Postmortem concentration is almost always higher than that during life; the concept of “therapeutic concentration” does not apply to a corpse.

Blood, urine and vitreous humour. Blood remains the main material: it is collected in a container with sodium fluoride. The concentration of ethanol in plasma is 10-15% higher than in whole blood. Heart blood is more sensitive than urine; GC/MS has become cheaper but is less specific; at autopsy there is often no urine in the bladder. The vitreous humour is protected from the external environment: it is reliable in those who drowned and after prolonged exposure. The amount of ethanol helps to distinguish postmortem formation from intake during life.

Hair, liver and stomach. A substance and its metabolites in hair are stable indefinitely; hair is easy to take and keep, and will give an answer if a question arises later. The liver is useful for drugs that bind strongly to protein. Because of diffusion from the stomach into the right lobe of the liver, only the left lobe is taken. For stomach examination to be meaningful, the volume must be recorded, the sample must be homogeneous, and the total amount calculated. No significance is attached to a low concentration, that is, the ion trap.

Interpreting the result: postmortem redistribution. Postmortem concentration cannot be interpreted in isolation: because of tolerance, the morphine concentration in a typical dependent person may be high. A substance in deep depots is released as the body decomposes. In a study on fentanyl, in 4 cases it was first stated “not detected”, and then the concentration rose to 52.5 µg/L. Because of redistribution the concentration is higher than that during life; therefore blood taken from the iliofemoral vessels is preferable.
